body.hook: Professional actors never walk on stage cold. Before a show, they stretch, breathe, hum and run tongue twisters, just like athletes before a game. A good warm-up prepares the body, voice and focus, and it protects your voice from strain.

vocabulary.definition: Activities that prepare the body, voice and mind for performance.
Using the diaphragm and core muscles to control the breath for speaking.
The dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that controls breathing.
Making the voice carry to the back of the space without shouting.
Shaping sounds clearly with the lips, teeth and tongue.
The richness of the voice created as sound vibrates in the chest and head.

study.title: Warm Up Like a Pro
study.question: How do actors prepare their bodies and voices?
study.passage:
Physical warm-up (5 minutes): Shake out hands, arms and legs; roll shoulders; gentle neck rolls (side to side, not all the way back); spine roll down and up, one vertebra at a time.
Breath (5 minutes): Lie on your back or stand with a hand on your belly. Breathe in through the nose for 4 counts, feeling the belly expand (not the shoulders rising). Breathe out on a "sss" for 8, then 12, then 16 counts.
Resonance (3 minutes): Hum with closed lips, feeling the buzz in your face. Slide the hum from low to high and back ("siren").
Articulation (5 minutes): Tongue twisters, slowly then faster: "Red leather, yellow leather." "Unique New York." "The tip of the tongue, the teeth, the lips."
Projection (5 minutes): Say a line ("Is anyone there?") to a partner 1 m away, then 5 m, then across the room, using breath support instead of throat strain.
Ensemble focus (5 minutes): Pass a sound and movement around the circle.
Leading: In groups of four, each student designs and leads a 5-minute warm-up for the group, including one physical, one breath, one vocal and one focus activity.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; tongue twisters are traditional.
